text.p: China successfully fired a meteorological satellite into orbit aboard a Long March 3 rocket on Tuesday, the official Xinhua news agency said.

The launch of domestically-produced Fengyun-2 satellite from the Xichang space centre in southwestern Sichuan province represented a mark of confidence for China's troubled space industry, which was shaken by a series f failures in 1995 and 1996.
The 1.38-tonne orbiter was launched toward synchronous orbit at 8.01 p.m. (1201 GMT), Xinhua said.

"Twenty-three minutes after the launching, the satellite and the rocket separated, and the satellite went into its predetermined orbit," the agency said. "It is reported that the satellite has been operating normally."
Chinese Premier Li Peng had showed great concern over the launch of China's first geostationary weather satellite and had repeatedly enquired about its progress, it said.
Top military officer and Politburo member Liu Huaqing had visited the launch site to inspect preparations, it said.

Fengyun-2 was launched less than a month after China put its troubled space industry back into gear by successfully launching the domestically-manufactured Dongfanghong-3 (East is Red) communications satellite.

That success, which prompted congratulations from the political and military leadership, was a welcome respite for an industry whose image as a low-cost high-quality launch provider had been tarnished by failures.
In February 1996, a Long March 3B rocket carrying a $230 million satellite for the global organisation Intelsat veered off course and exploded, killing at least six people and injuring more than 50.
In August, a U.S.-built communications satellite failed to reach proper orbit after its launch on a Long March 3A rocket.

Chinese space officials said last month that a successful launch of the Fengyun-2, which is intended to improve weather forecasting and help predict natural disasters, could be followed by other launches for foreign customers.
Officials of China Aerospace Corp have said they plan to use the Long March rocket family to loft more than 30 satellites into orbit for overseas clients over the next four years.
International insurers have said a series of successful launches is essential to bring down insurance costs sent soaring by last year's failures.
China's eagerness to bolster its launch image has been reflected in a spate of articles in the state-controlled press praising recent successes involving domestic commercial and research satellites.

The Fengyun-2 orbiter was developed mainly by the Shanghai Aerospace Technology Research Institute under the China Aerospace Corporation and was designed to have a life span of three years, Xinhua said.
The second-generation meteorological satellite was equipped with a scanning radiometer, cloud coverage information system and a data collection translator, it said.

The satellite could provide cloud maps and information on temperature and wind movements over China and its neighbouring countries from its orbit over the equator at 105 degrees east longitude, it said.
